name: REVEREND SOWERBY
note: SOWERBY AT THE JUDGES' TABLE, holding the pencil. Doc 57 F4: 'The first time Thad steps onto the street after T_ASSAY_RUN, Fanshawe is waiting with half the town and the judges' table on the boardwalk, Sowerby holding the pencil.' Cut from room-02 operations 1 and 2 by tools/art/room02-duel-cast.py and laid over Room 2's own street. Present for the visit the duel is called on (T_DUEL_CROWD), and gone the next time.
barksNote: The duel is spoken through the assay (content/assay/assay.json).

sprite.frameNote: 0 the pencil raised · 1 breath (derived) · 2 the pencil lowered · 3 leaning to confer · 4 the pencil held high.
sprite.redrawn: Errata 111 T (Tyler, 2026-11-06: no table at Duel Three; the gathering composed as one picture). Drawn standing on magenta from the locked cast master by cast-unify operation 28 (reference/cast-unify-26.txt), turned toward the duel, cut with its own pixels and a clean edge; placed where the painted composition (cast-unify 27, art/staging/cast-unify/batch-25/edit-porch.png) stood him, feet on the boards or the street, drawn at the street's man there.

placedNote: On the hotel porch's boards right of its corner post (the post is x 2860-2885), well back from the front edge -- not at the porch's corner by the barrel, where Tyler saw him floating ('the guy to the right of the porch is floating off the edge of the porch').

standsOn.surface: the hotel porch, right of its corner post
standsOn.note: The hotel porch's boards, measured on the plate (renders/main-street-porch-floor@6x.png): from the foot of the wall (y 584-594) to the front edge (y 604-606). Feet are inside it, so he stands ON the boards -- first placed at y 572, on the foot of the wall, and he hovered in front of it (Tyler: 'They're floating over the porch').

facesNote: Toward the duel: Fanshawe and Thad below, Thad to the right. Measured on the rest frame by tests/faces.test.mjs.

leaves.note: Errata 131 F: after the hat (doc 03, Duel Four), the crowd and the judges go. They have no walk (errata 99 N), so they fade rather than vanish (Tyler, 2026-11-01: never just disappear).
